title: Short Stuff: Skittles and TIO2
summary: Short Stuff installment on Skittles and titanium dioxide. Chuck covers a July 2022 California class action lawsuit against Mars Incorporated over titanium dioxide in Skittles, which he says was dismissed without prejudice in November 2022, and a second suit by another woman in summer 2023. Josh notes Mars said in 2016 it would phase out titanium dioxide from its candies, yet Skittles still contained it in 2024, and that the additive can be listed simply as titanium dioxide. The hosts explain titanium dioxide as a naturally occurring whitening and light-scattering agent used in food, sunscreen, makeup and toothpaste, and discuss nanoparticles and the basis of the health concerns. They note the evidence is mostly from animal studies, with no proof of harm in humans from eating it. They cover FDA rules (up to one percent of food weight), the EU and Dunkin' Donuts removing it in 2015 from powdered donut toppings, an Environmental Working Group paper on children's sweets, and a National Poison Control Center estimate that about one-tenth of one percent passes through the gut. They close by questioning why Skittles contain it at all.

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Short Stuff episode with Chuck.

segments.title: Skittles lawsuit against Mars
segments.summary: Chuck describes a July 2022 California class action against Mars Incorporated over titanium dioxide in Skittles, which he says was dismissed without prejudice in November 2022, and a second suit filed in summer 2023 whose status is unknown.

segments.title: Mars phase-out pledge and labeling
segments.summary: Josh notes Mars pledged in 2016 to phase out titanium dioxide from its candies, yet Skittles still contained it in 2024, and that the additive can be listed simply as titanium dioxide. The hosts question the reversal.

segments.title: What titanium dioxide is and where it is used
segments.summary: Chuck explains that titanium dioxide forms when titanium reacts with oxygen, forming a fine white powder used as a whitening agent in processed foods, sunscreen, makeup and toothpaste.

segments.title: Nanoparticles and light scattering
segments.summary: Josh explains that titanium dioxide reflects light strongly, and the food use involves nanoparticles around 100 nanometers across, which scatter light more effectively when smaller and can potentially travel through the body.

segments.title: Bloodstream, organ accumulation and the color question
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether nanoparticles can enter the bloodstream and accumulate in organs such as the liver and kidneys. Josh says there is no pure evidence of that, and cites the Titanium Dioxide Manufacturers Association's claim that food-grade titanium dioxide is not shown to be harmful.

segments.title: Evidence limits and skepticism
segments.summary: Josh says the research is almost entirely animal, mostly mouse, studies showing damage, plus human inflammation when inhaled; eating it differs. He argues skepticism is warranted given xenobiotics and food industry history, though no smoking gun exists.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief break with jokes before the sponsor read and return.

segments.title: Sponsor read or theme bumper
segments.summary: Short theme bumper and tagline played during the break.

segments.title: FDA rules and EU and Dunkin' Donuts removal
segments.summary: Chuck says the FDA allows titanium dioxide as a food additive up to one percent of food weight. He notes Dunkin' Donuts stopped using it in 2015 in powdered donut toppings and that the EU has moved to remove it.

segments.title: Children, Environmental Working Group and gut absorption
segments.summary: Josh cites an Environmental Working Group paper saying the additive is in thousands of children's sweets and that smaller bodies may be more affected. He says a National Poison Control Center source estimates about one-tenth of one percent passes through the gut, and that no studies yet show harm.

segments.title: Why it is in Skittles
segments.summary: The hosts say they do not understand the purpose in Skittles. Josh says sources describe it as a color or flavor enhancer, and jokes about mustard-flavored Skittles.

segments.title: Closing thoughts on candy
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the unlikely appearance of a bag of Skittles and admit they like candy, including Skittles and Starburst, which contain the additive.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh closes the Short Stuff episode and gives the production credit.
